title: Little Bethlehem (Micah 5:2)
hookLine: from the least of the clans shall come a ruler

cards: Every country has towns like this. Not the capital, not the place on the postcards. A village you'd drive through on the way to somewhere else, where the gas station closes at six.
Ancient Judah had one about six miles south of Jerusalem. Its one claim to fame was centuries old: a shepherd boy named David grew up there before he became king.
Otherwise, a farming village on a hillside, with a homely name. Bethlehem is usually explained as house of bread. And Micah, the same prophet as yesterday, looked at it and said: watch this place.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting."
Ephratah was the old name of the clan and district around the village, telling it apart from another Bethlehem in the north. And look at little.

Micah doesn't pretend Bethlehem is impressive; it's one of the least of Judah's clans. That's the point. Jerusalem in Micah's day was full of powerful people, and Micah has hard words for many of them.
So the hope for a good ruler doesn't come from the palace.

It comes from the hillside, from David's humble start. Jews have read this as a promise of a future king from David's family, and many still hold that hope. Christians read it as fulfilled in Jesus, born in Bethlehem.
In Matthew's Gospel, when foreign wise men arrive asking where the king is to be born, Herod's scholars quote Micah.
And Matthew's version has a lovely twist: where Micah says little, Matthew's quotation says "not the least."

teach.h: YET OUT OF THEE SHALL HE COME FORTH.
teach.b: The birth changes the town's standing. This whole week has had that shape: Amos's river; Jonah running, praying, watching his enemies turn, sulking at mercy; Micah's three things; and now a little town.
Over and over, God doesn't start where the power is.

how: Micah 5:2 is read in many churches during Advent and at Christmas services of lessons and carols, and it is quoted in Matthew 2 in the story of the wise men.

games.q: you're Herod's scholars. foreign visitors ask where the promised king is to be born. where do you send them?
games.why: they quote Micah and point to Bethlehem, the little town, as Matthew 2 tells it.

practice: Think of a small place that shaped you, a grandparent's kitchen, a back road, a classroom with a broken heater, or a small daily thing like the first cup of coffee.

Picture it in detail, the smell, the light, the people, and let it be important for a minute, the way Micah let Bethlehem be important. If you pray, give thanks for that place and its people; if not, simply hold it with gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Little Bethlehem. A small farming village, David's hometown, where Micah said a ruler would come from, and where the Gospels say Jesus was born.

orig.note: Hebrew: Bethlehem, usually explained as house of bread.

carryVoice: Your line: the least of the towns. Little, and then not the least. Day four hundred ninety, and another week on the path.
